To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
attrition in a longitudinal study of neuropsychology in childhood cancer is not random and that, in this study, the attrition is not likely to be a major source of bias.

(1) attrition in longitudinal studies of neuropsychological change in children with cancer is substantial, and (2) missing data can be handled by using multiple imputation methods, and that this method is preferable to the traditional approach of dropping cases with missing data from analyses.
attrition in longitudinal studies can be handled in a variety of ways that differ in their effects on parameter estimates and statistical tests, and that these effects can be substantial.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of cancer on the cognitive and academic functioning of children, the effects of disease relapse on neuropsychological outcome, and the effects of treatment variables on neuropsychological functioning.
the problem of missing data in a longitudinal study of neuropsychologic outcome in pediatric cancer.
the treatment of missing data and its effect on longitudinal studies of children with cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, it is not optimal to drop incomplete cases from analyses in longitudinal research, and that, in particular, the data presented in this study suggest that the use of maximum likelihood estimation with missing values imputed by expectation maximization is a useful strategy to deal with missing data in repeated-measures designs.
the results of the present study suggest that attrition is not likely to have a major impact on the results of longitudinal studies of neuropsychological change in children with cancer.

the results of this study suggest that, in longitudinal studies with children and adults, missing data should be treated as missing at random and should be imputed using a maximum likelihood procedure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a multiple imputation procedure to deal with missing data is preferable to the more common practice of dropping incomplete cases from the analysis.
the effects of missing data on the analysis of longitudinal data are substantial.
the data presented have shown that the neuropsychological outcome of childhood cancer is better than previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that

researchers should not simply drop incomplete cases, but rather should use the available data to make the best estimates of population parameters and the most powerful tests of statistical hypotheses possible.
researchers should be cautious about excluding cases with incomplete data from analyses.
researchers conducting longitudinal studies with pediatric cancer patients should not drop incomplete cases.
